newsitem.title: UK: China leadership seen steady, for now, after Deng.
newsitem.headline: China leadership seen steady, for now, after Deng.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

China's communist leadership will close ranks following the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping but power struggles may well be on the way as Beijing tries to deal with explosive change in the country, Western diplomats and analysts say.

Party chief Jiang Zemin will take over the leadership for now, a move that has been carefully prepared during Deng's long illness -- meaning little change in Chinese policy at home or abroad in the next weeks and months.

Beyond that, however, the leadership faces difficult decisions on a whole range of issues affecting the country's 1.2 billion people and neighbouring countries which are already nervous about China's growing assertiveness.
"I don't think anybody expects bloody conflict... but the struggle (for power) will be joined in a very serious way," said Gerald Segal of the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London.

"This is the passing of an era and the question is whether the leadership has enough to keep it united in the medium-term, when there are so many challenges," said Peter Ferdinand of Britain's Warwick University.
For now at least -- and probably until the Chinese communist party's 15th Congress due in October -- Jiang is expected to hold the reins of power.

"The orderly succession has been long planned and no one expects things to change very much on important issues like the economic programme, the return of Hong Kong and so on," said one Western diplomat.

U.S. officials in Washington said they expected Deng's death would have little effect on the functioning of the country, while Secretary of State Madeleine Albright -- who will visit China next week -- said she hoped for a smooth transition of power in the world's most populous country.

Jiang, who is also state president and head of the army, has taken care to build up a solid power base after a shaky start when he was first promoted in the wake of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.
While his stature does not even approach the reverence accorded to Deng, he is certainly seen as the first among equals in the leadership.

Nevertheless, Chinese leaders have already been jockeying for position behind the scenes, pushing a harder line against domestic dissent and on foreign policy issues like Taiwan and Hong Kong to avoid appearing weak at home.

Deng turned China into a booming powerhouse through economic liberalisation but firmly believed in keeping political control through the Communist party -- as the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and crackdown on dissent showed.

The problem that his successors face, analysts say, is how to deal with the consequences of economic freedom, which fuel demand for greater political freedoms, while keeping some degree of central political control.
Diplomats say there is already a debate within the Chinese leadership over whether to go even further with reforms or whether to slow the pace in the name of law and order.
"Beijing is already losing control over the richer regions," said Ferdinand.

"You now have problems of unemployment, corruption, crime, drugs, huge disparities of wealth between some of the regions. No one wanted to deal with this, or question Deng's authority, while he was alive."
With such challenges ahead, the leadership knows that it must stick together for now in order to survive.

"These people saw what happened to the Soviet Union," said Ferdinand. "The question is whether solidarity will carry them through the challenges, the antagonism and rivalries that are there below the surface."
Segal questioned whether Jiang, without the revered age and revolutionary credentials of Deng, would be able to exert authority in the new China.
"This is the first time China will have a leader who is... a grey bureaucrat...," he said. "(The leadership) will be much weaker at a time when the changes are enormous."
